intro: The Torah ends with Moses looking at the land from a mountain. This unit begins on the other side of the river. The books of Joshua and Judges tell how the people came into the land and how they lived there, tribe by tribe, with no king. Leaders called judges stepped up when trouble came. Some were wise, like Deborah. Some were brave, like Gideon. Some were strong but made big mistakes, like Samson.

Then the unit turns to two families. In the book of Ruth, a young woman from Moab chooses to stay with her mother-in-law. In the first book of Samuel, a woman named Hannah prays for a son. That son, Samuel, grows up to hear a voice in the night and to lead the people. At the end, the people ask him for a king.

In this unit you will learn where these books sit in the Tanakh, what they say, and how Jewish readers have read them. You will meet a Hebrew word, chesed, that means loyal kindness. And you will practice saying "the text says" and "Jewish tradition teaches" when you tell what you found.
bigQuestion: What do the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth and 1 Samuel say about courage, loyalty and the kind of leader a people needs?

a ram's horn blown like a trumpet; seven were blown at Jericho

test.q: Which book is the first in Nevi'im, the Prophets?
test.why: The Tanakh's second part, Nevi'im, begins with the book of Joshua, right after the Torah.

test.q: Who hid the two spies on her roof in Jericho?
test.why: Joshua 2 says Rahab of Jericho hid the spies and was kept safe when the city fell.

test.q: What does the book of Joshua say the people did at Jericho for six days?
choices: Marched around the city once a day
test.why: Joshua 6 says the people marched around Jericho once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh.

test.q: Which tribe got towns spread across the land instead of one big share?
test.why: The book of Joshua says the Levites, who helped with worship, got towns in every tribe's land.

test.q: In the book of Judges, what did a judge do?
choices: Ruled as king from a palace
Stepped up to lead in a crisis
test.why: The judges were rescuers and leaders in a crisis; the book says there was no king in those days.

test.q: Who went to battle only after Deborah agreed to go too?
test.why: Judges 4:8 says Barak would go only if Deborah went with him.

test.q: How many men did Gideon keep after the test at the stream?
test.why: Judges 7 says only three hundred lapped water from their hands, and Gideon kept them.

test.q: Which people did Samson fight, according to the book of Judges?
test.why: Samson's enemies in Judges 13–16 are the Philistines, who lived by the sea.

test.q: What is the last line of the book of Judges about?
choices: There was no king, and everyone did what seemed right to them
test.why: Judges 21:25 says there was no king in Israel and every person did what was right in their own eyes.

test.q: What did Ruth say to Naomi on the road?
choices: I will go back to Moab
Where you go, I will go
test.why: Ruth 1:16 says: whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people.

test.q: In which part of the Tanakh is the book of Ruth found?
test.why: Ruth is one of the five Megillot in Ketuvim, the Writings, and is read on Shavuot.

test.q: What was Ruth doing in Boaz's field?
test.why: Ruth 2 says Ruth gleaned, gathering grain the harvesters left, as the Torah allows for the poor.

test.q: What did Hannah promise about her son?
choices: He would serve God all his life
test.why: 1 Samuel 1:11 says Hannah promised to give her son to serve God, and she brought Samuel to Shiloh.

test.q: What did Samuel say when the voice called him the fourth time?
choices: Where you go, I will go
Speak, for your servant is listening
test.why: 1 Samuel 3:10 says Samuel answered as Eli taught him: speak, for Thy servant heareth.

test.q: What did Samuel warn a king would take from the people?
choices: Their sons, daughters, fields and crops
test.why: In 1 Samuel 8, Samuel lists what a king takes: sons, daughters, the best fields and a tenth of the crops.

write.prompt: What kind of leader do these books say a people needs? Pick two people from the unit, like Deborah (Judges 4), Gideon (Judges 7), Ruth (Ruth 1) or Samuel (1 Samuel 3 or 8). For each, tell what the text says they did and what Jewish readers have seen in it. Then say what the two stories have in common.
tips: Name the book and chapter each time you tell part of a story, like "Judges 7 says."
Say "the text says" for what happens and "Jewish tradition teaches" for what readers have taken from it.
Use two words from the unit, like judge, chesed, haftarah or anoint.
Compare the two people. Do not say one is good and one is bad; say what each one did.
Keep your sentences short. One idea in each sentence.

title: Into the Land

chapters.title: Joshua, Deborah, Gideon, Samson
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the books of Joshua and Judges say about courage, trust and choices?

story.title: The Judge Under the Palm Tree
story.kicker: People walk for miles up a hill road, because a woman under a tree will tell them what is right.
paragraphs: The sun is hot on the hill road. A farmer and his neighbor walk side by side, but they do not talk. They have been arguing for weeks about a goat. Whose goat is it? They cannot agree. So they are walking to the palm tree.

Everyone in the hills of Ephraim knows the tree. The book of Judges says a woman named Deborah sat under it. She was a prophetess, a person the text says spoke for God. She was also a judge. People came from all over to ask her what was right.

The two men reach the top of the hill. Under the wide palm leaves sits Deborah. She does not hurry. She listens to the farmer. She listens to the neighbor. She asks questions. Then she gives her answer, and both men nod. The argument is over.

The book of Judges says Deborah did more than settle arguments. When an enemy army came, she called a leader named Barak. She told him to gather ten thousand men. He said he would go only if she went too. She went.

This chapter is about leaders like Deborah. The Tanakh calls them judges. They were not kings. They were people who stepped up in a crisis. Some were wise. Some were brave. Some made big mistakes. Their stories are in the book of Judges, right after the book of Joshua.
story.think: Why do you think people walked so far to ask Deborah what was right? What makes a person someone others trust?

lessons.title: A New Leader Named Joshua
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Joshua says Joshua led the people into the land after Moses died, and was told to be strong and brave.
reading: The Torah ends with the death of Moses. The next book in the Tanakh is *Joshua*. It is the first book of the *Nevi'im*, the Prophets. Jewish tradition calls Joshua and Judges the Former Prophets. They tell the story of the people after Moses.

The book of Joshua says Joshua had been Moses' helper for many years. Now he became the leader. The text says God spoke to him. God told him to cross the Jordan River into the land. God told him three times to be strong and have courage.

The people crossed the Jordan. The book says the water stopped, like at the sea in Exodus. They set up twelve stones to remember it, one for each tribe. Then they were in the land the Torah had promised to Abraham.

words.d: the leader after Moses; also the first book of the Prophets in the Tanakh
the Prophets, the second part of the Tanakh; it begins with Joshua

look.title: Be Strong and Brave
look.text: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
look.prompt: The old words "thee" and "thou" mean "you." What is Joshua told to do? What reason is he given?

check.q: Which part of the Tanakh does the book of Joshua begin?
check.why: Joshua is the first book of Nevi'im, the Prophets, which comes right after the Torah.

check.q: Who led the people before Joshua, according to the text?
check.why: The Torah ends with Moses' death, and the book of Joshua says Joshua, his helper, became leader.

check.q: What does the book of Joshua say God told Joshua to be?
check.why: Joshua 1 says God told Joshua three times to be strong and have courage.

lessons.title: The Walls of Jericho
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Joshua says the people marched around Jericho for seven days, and the walls fell.
reading: The first city in the land was *Jericho*. It had a high wall all around it. Before the people crossed the river, Joshua sent two spies. A woman in Jericho named Rahab hid them on her roof. She asked them to keep her family safe. They promised.

The book of Joshua tells what happened next. The people marched around the city once a day for six days. Priests carried the ark of the covenant. Seven priests blew ram's horns, called *shofarot*. No one spoke. On the seventh day they marched seven times.

Then the priests blew, and all the people shouted. The text says the wall fell down flat. The people took the city. Rahab and her family were kept safe, as promised. Jewish readers have long told this story. The Talmud even remembers Rahab as a person who joined the people of Israel.

words.d: the walled city the book of Joshua says was the first taken in the land
a ram's horn blown like a trumpet; the plural is shofarot
the woman of Jericho who hid the spies and was kept safe

look.title: Seven Days Around Jericho
look.unit: as the book of Joshua counts them
look.prompt: How many times did the people walk around Jericho in all? Add the six days and the seventh day.

check.q: Who hid the two spies in Jericho?
check.why: Joshua 2 says Rahab of Jericho hid the spies on her roof and asked them to keep her family safe.

check.q: What is a shofar?
choices: A ram's horn blown like a trumpet
check.why: A shofar is a ram's horn. The book of Joshua says seven priests blew shofarot at Jericho.

check.q: What does the book of Joshua say happened on the seventh day at Jericho?
choices: The wall fell down after the shout
check.why: Joshua 6 says the people marched seven times, shouted, and the wall fell down flat.

lessons.title: Land for the Tribes
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Joshua says the land was divided among the tribes of Israel, and Joshua gave a farewell speech.
reading: The people of Israel were made of twelve *tribes*. A tribe is a big family group. Each tribe came from one of Jacob's sons. The book of Joshua says the land was divided among them. Each tribe got its own part to live in and farm.

One tribe was different. The tribe of Levi did not get a big piece of land. The text says the Levites helped with worship instead. They got towns spread all over the land. Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, each got a part of their own.

At the end of the book, Joshua is old. He gathers the people at a place called Shechem. He tells the story of Abraham, Egypt and the crossing. He asks the people to choose to serve God. The text says the people answer that they will.

words.d: a large family group; the book says Israel had twelve tribes, each from a son of Jacob
the tribe of Levi, who the text says helped with worship and got towns instead of a big land share

look.title: One Tribe, Many Towns
look.text: Picture a map with twelve big shapes on it. Each shape has a tribe's name: Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, Dan, and more. Now look closer. Small dots are scattered inside every shape. The dots are towns for the tribe of Levi. The Levites did not get one big shape. They got dots in everyone's land.
look.prompt: Why might it help to have the Levites, who led worship, living in every part of the land instead of in one place?

check.q: How many tribes of Israel does the text name?
check.why: Israel had twelve tribes, each from a son of Jacob, and the book of Joshua divides the land among them.

check.q: Which tribe did not get a big share of land, according to the book of Joshua?
check.why: The text says the Levites helped with worship and got towns spread across the land instead.

check.q: What does Joshua ask the people to do at Shechem?
check.why: In Joshua 24, Joshua retells the story and asks the people to choose to serve God, and they say they will.

lessons.title: What a Judge Did
lessons.mainIdea: In the book of Judges, a judge was a leader who stepped up in a crisis, not a king.
reading: After Joshua died, there was no one leader. The book of *Judges* says the people lived tribe by tribe. Again and again, trouble came. An enemy would attack. The text says the people would cry out. Then a leader would step up. That leader was called a judge.

A judge in this book is not a person in a courtroom. A judge was a rescuer. Some led armies. Some settled arguments. Some did both. When the crisis was over, the judge did not become king. There was no palace and no crown.

The book of Judges has a pattern. It says the people turned away from God. Trouble came. The people cried out. A judge saved them. There was peace for a while. Then it happened again. Readers call this the *cycle* of Judges.

words.d: the book after Joshua; also the leaders in it who stepped up in a crisis
a pattern that happens over and over; in Judges: trouble, crying out, a judge, peace, then trouble again

look.title: Four Books, Many Chapters
look.cite: Chapter counts in the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh, 1917
look.prompt: Which book is shortest? Which two books together have more chapters than 1 Samuel?

check.q: In the book of Judges, what was a judge?
choices: A leader who stepped up in a crisis
check.why: The judges were rescuers and leaders in a crisis, not kings; the text says there was no king then.

check.q: What is the cycle of Judges?
choices: A pattern of trouble, crying out, a judge, and peace
check.why: Readers call the repeating pattern in the book the cycle: trouble, crying out, a judge, peace, then trouble again.

check.q: What happened after a judge saved the people, according to the book?
choices: There was peace for a while, then trouble again
check.why: The book says there was peace for a time, and then the pattern started over. Judges did not become kings.

lessons.title: Deborah Under the Palm Tree
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Judges says Deborah was a prophetess and judge who led the people with Barak against an enemy army.
reading: The book of Judges says *Deborah* was a prophetess. That means the text says she spoke for God. She was also a judge. She sat under a palm tree in the hills of Ephraim. People came to her to settle their arguments.

An enemy king named Jabin ruled over the people. His general was Sisera, who had nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah sent for Barak. She told him to gather ten thousand men. *Barak* said he would go only if Deborah went with him. She said she would.

The text says a big rain came and the chariots got stuck in the mud. Barak's men won. Sisera ran away on foot to a tent. A woman named Jael was there, and the text says she killed him. Judges 5 is a long song of Deborah. Many scholars think it is one of the oldest poems in the Tanakh.

words.d: a prophetess and judge in the book of Judges who sat under a palm tree
the army leader Deborah called; he would go only if she went too
a woman the text says spoke for God

look.title: Deborah's Palm Tree
look.text: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, she judged Israel at that time. And she sat under the palm-tree of Deborah between Ramah and Beth-el in the hill-country of Ephraim; and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment.
look.prompt: Find two jobs the text gives Deborah. Where did people go to see her?

check.q: Where does the book of Judges say Deborah sat?
choices: In a boat on the river
check.why: Judges 4:5 says Deborah sat under a palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim, and people came to her.

check.q: What did Barak say when Deborah told him to fight?
choices: He said he was too old
He would go only if she went too
He asked for a king first
check.why: Judges 4:8 says Barak would go only if Deborah went with him, and she did.

check.q: What is Judges chapter 5?
check.why: Judges 5 is the Song of Deborah, which many scholars think is one of the oldest poems in the Tanakh.

lessons.title: Gideon's Small Army
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Judges says Gideon won with only three hundred men, so the people would trust God and not their numbers.
reading: The book of Judges says a people called the Midianites came every year. They took the crops. A man named *Gideon* was hiding wheat from them. The text says a messenger from God called him a mighty man of valor. Gideon did not feel mighty. He asked for signs first.

Gideon gathered an army of thirty-two thousand men. The text says God told him the army was too big. If they won, they would say they did it by themselves. Gideon sent home everyone who was afraid. Twenty-two thousand left. Ten thousand stayed.

That was still too many. The text says God had Gideon watch the men drink from a stream. Only three hundred lapped water from their hands. Gideon kept those three hundred. At night they blew horns, broke jars and held up torches. The Midianite camp panicked and ran.

words.d: the judge in the book of Judges who fought the Midianites with three hundred men
the people the book of Judges says raided Israel's crops in Gideon's time

look.title: Gideon's Shrinking Army
look.unit: men, as the book of Judges counts them
look.prompt: The text gives a reason the army had to be small. What was it? Look at how much smaller 300 is than 32,000.

check.q: Why does the text say Gideon's army had to be small?
choices: So the people would not say they won by themselves
check.why: Judges 7:2 says the army was too big, or the people would claim they had won on their own.

check.q: How many men did Gideon keep, according to the book of Judges?
check.why: After the test at the stream, Gideon kept the three hundred men who lapped water from their hands.

check.q: What did Gideon's men carry into the camp at night?
check.why: Judges 7 says the men blew horns, broke jars and held up torches, and the camp panicked.

lessons.title: Samson's Strength
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Judges says Samson was set apart as a Nazirite from birth and was very strong.
reading: The book of Judges tells about *Samson*. Before he was born, the text says a messenger came to his mother. Her child would be a *Nazirite*. A Nazirite made special promises. He did not drink wine. He did not cut his hair. Samson was set apart from birth.

Samson grew up very strong. The text says he tore a lion apart with his hands. He fought the *Philistines*, a people who lived by the sea. Once he caught three hundred foxes and tied torches to their tails to burn the Philistines' fields.

The Philistines tried to tie him up. The text says he broke the ropes like burned string. He fought a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey. The book says Samson judged Israel for twenty years. But he was not wise like Deborah. He acted first and thought later.

words.d: the very strong judge in the book of Judges who fought the Philistines
a person set apart by special promises, such as not cutting hair or drinking wine
a people who lived by the sea and, the text says, fought Israel in Samson's time

look.title: Strong, but Wise?
look.text: Read two lines about two judges. Deborah: people came to her, she listened, and then she gave an answer. Samson: he saw something he wanted, and he grabbed it. He got angry, and he struck. Both are called judges in the same book.
look.prompt: What kind of strength does each one have? Which kind do you think the book wants readers to notice?

check.q: What was a Nazirite?
choices: A soldier with an iron chariot
A person set apart by special promises
A judge who sat under a tree
check.why: A Nazirite made promises like not cutting hair or drinking wine; the text says Samson was one from birth.

check.q: Which people does the book of Judges say Samson fought?
check.why: Samson's enemies in Judges 13–16 are the Philistines, a people who lived by the sea.

check.q: How is Samson different from Deborah in the book?
choices: He acted first and thought later
check.why: Deborah listened and judged; Samson used his strength quickly and often did not think first.

lessons.title: Samson's Mistakes
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Judges says Samson gave away his secret, lost his strength, and made one last choice.
reading: Samson loved a woman named *Delilah*. The Philistine leaders paid her to find the secret of his strength. Three times Samson told her a false answer. Three times the Philistines tried and failed. Delilah kept asking, day after day.

At last Samson told her the truth. He was a Nazirite. His hair had never been cut. The text says Delilah had his hair cut while he slept. His strength left him. The Philistines caught him and blinded him. They made him grind grain in a prison in Gaza.

The Philistines held a big feast for their god Dagon. They brought Samson out to laugh at him. The text says his hair had begun to grow. He asked to lean on the two middle pillars. He pushed, and the building fell on everyone, including him. The book calls this his last act.

words.d: the woman the book of Judges says was paid to learn the secret of Samson's strength
the Philistine city where the text says Samson was held in prison

look.title: The Secret Told
look.text: In Judges 16:17, Samson finally tells Delilah everything. He says a razor has never touched his head. He has been a Nazirite to God since he was born. If his hair were shaved, his strength would leave him, and he would be weak like any other man.
look.cite: Judges 16:17, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: Samson had already lied to Delilah three times. Why do you think he told the truth this time? What does the story say about trust?

check.q: What secret did Samson finally tell Delilah?
choices: His hair had never been cut
check.why: Judges 16:17 says Samson told her he was a Nazirite and his hair had never been cut.

check.q: What did the Philistines do after Samson lost his strength?
choices: Blinded him and put him in prison
check.why: The book says the Philistines blinded Samson and made him grind grain in a prison in Gaza.

check.q: How many times did Samson give Delilah a false answer?
check.why: Judges 16 says Samson lied three times before he told Delilah the truth.

lessons.title: No King in Those Days
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Judges ends with a line that says there was no king, and everyone did what seemed right to them.
reading: The last line of the book of Judges is famous. It says that in those days there was no *king* in Israel. Every person did what was right in their own eyes. The book says this line four times near the end. It is a kind of sad sigh.

Readers have long asked what the line means. Some say it is a wish for a king who would bring order. The next books, Samuel and Kings, are about kings. Other readers say the line is a warning. When everyone decides alone, things can go wrong.

The stories at the end of Judges are hard. There is fighting between tribes. People do cruel things. The text does not cheer for them. It tells them plainly. Jewish tradition reads these chapters as a lesson about what happens when a people loses its way.

words.d: a ruler over a whole people; the book of Judges says Israel had none in those days
the way a person sees things; doing what seems right to you alone

look.title: The Last Line of Judges
look.text: In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
look.prompt: Is this line a wish, a warning, or both? What in the book makes you think so?

check.q: How does the book of Judges end?
choices: With a line saying there was no king
check.why: Judges 21:25 says there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

check.q: Which books come after Judges and tell about kings?
check.why: The books of Samuel and Kings tell how Israel got kings, starting with Saul.

check.q: How do some readers understand the last line of Judges?
choices: As a warning about everyone deciding alone
As a map of the tribes
check.why: Many readers see the line as a warning: when there is no shared leader, people can lose their way.

lessons.title: Courage, Trust and Choices
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish readers have found lessons about courage, trust and good choices in the stories of Joshua and Judges.
reading: The stories in this chapter show different kinds of *courage*. Joshua is told to be strong and brave. Rahab risks her life to hide the spies. Deborah goes to battle when Barak asks. Gideon is afraid at first, but he goes. Courage in these books does not mean having no fear.

The stories also show *trust*. Gideon's army is made small so the people will trust God, not their numbers. The book of Judges says trouble came when the people forgot. Jewish tradition reads these stories on some Shabbat mornings as a *haftarah*, a reading from the Prophets after the Torah portion.

The rabbis had a saying about strength. In Pirkei Avot, a book of rabbis' sayings, Ben Zoma asks who is strong. His answer is the person who controls their own urges. Many Jewish readers think of Samson here. He could lift a city gate, but he could not control himself. That is the choice the stories ask about.

words.d: doing what is right even when you are afraid
believing someone will keep their word; in these books, trust in God's promise
a reading from the Prophets read in synagogue after the Torah portion

look.title: Who Is Strong?
look.text: In Pirkei Avot 4:1, the sage Ben Zoma asks: Who is mighty? His answer: the one who controls their own urges. He points to Proverbs 16:32, which says a person slow to anger is better than a mighty warrior, and one who rules their spirit is better than one who takes a city.
look.cite: Pirkei Avot 4:1, paraphrased from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: By Ben Zoma's measure, was Samson strong? Was Deborah? Explain using one story from this chapter.

check.q: What is a haftarah?
choices: A reading from the Prophets after the Torah portion
check.why: A haftarah is a passage from Nevi'im, the Prophets, read in synagogue after the Torah reading.

check.q: In Pirkei Avot, who does Ben Zoma say is strong?
choices: The one with the biggest army
The one who can lift a gate
The one who never feels afraid
The one who controls their own urges
check.why: Ben Zoma's saying in Pirkei Avot 4:1 defines strength as ruling over your own urges.

check.q: What do these stories say courage means?
choices: Doing what is right even when afraid
check.why: Gideon was afraid and Barak wanted Deborah beside him, yet both went. Courage here is acting despite fear.

review.q: Which book comes right after the Torah in the Tanakh?
review.why: Joshua is the first book of Nevi'im, the Prophets, which follows the Torah.

review.q: What does the book of Joshua say fell at Jericho?
review.why: Joshua 6 says the wall fell down flat after the horns blew and the people shouted.

review.q: Which tribe got towns instead of one big share of land?
review.why: The book of Joshua says the Levites, who helped with worship, got towns spread across the land.

review.q: Which judge was a prophetess who sat under a palm tree?
review.why: Judges 4 says Deborah, a prophetess, judged Israel under a palm tree in Ephraim.

review.q: How many men did Gideon take into the Midianite camp?
review.why: Judges 7 says Gideon kept three hundred men after the test at the stream.

review.q: Which promise was part of being a Nazirite?
review.why: Samson was a Nazirite, and the text says his hair had never been cut.

review.q: Who was paid to learn the secret of Samson's strength?
review.why: Judges 16 says the Philistine leaders paid Delilah to find out the secret.

review.q: What is the cycle in the book of Judges?
choices: Trouble, crying out, a judge, peace, then trouble again
review.why: The book repeats a pattern: the people forget, trouble comes, they cry out, a judge saves them, and peace lasts a while.

chapters.title: Ruth, Hannah and Samuel
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the stories of Ruth, Hannah and Samuel show loyalty and kindness, and how did Israel come to ask for a king?

story.title: A Promise on a Dusty Road
story.kicker: Three women stand at a crossroads. One is going home. The other two must choose.
paragraphs: The road is dry and dusty. It runs from the land of Moab toward Bethlehem, a town in the hills of Judah. An old woman named Naomi stands on the road. Two young women stand with her. They are her sons' wives. Her sons have died. Her husband has died. She has nothing left in Moab.

Naomi turns to the two young women. Their names are Orpah and Ruth. Go back, she tells them. Go home to your mothers. You are young. You can marry again. I am old and I have nothing to give you. She kisses them. All three of them cry.

Orpah kisses Naomi and turns back toward Moab. She has made her choice, and the book of Ruth does not blame her. But Ruth does not move. She holds on to Naomi. Naomi tells her again to go. Ruth answers with words that people still say today.

Do not ask me to leave you, Ruth says. Where you go, I will go. Where you sleep, I will sleep. Your people will be my people. Your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die. Naomi sees that Ruth means it. She stops arguing. The two women walk on together.

This chapter begins with Ruth's promise. It is the story of a stranger who chose to stay. Then it turns to another woman, Hannah, who prayed for a child. Her son Samuel would grow up to lead Israel. And the chapter ends with the people asking for something new: a king.
story.think: Ruth could have gone home like Orpah. Why do you think she stayed with Naomi instead? What did it cost her?

lessons.title: A Famine and a Journey
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ruth says a family left Bethlehem in a famine, and Naomi came back with only Ruth beside her.
reading: The book of *Ruth* is short. It has only four chapters. It begins in the days when the judges judged. There was a famine, a time with no food. A man from Bethlehem took his wife *Naomi* and two sons to the land of Moab. Moab was across the Dead Sea, to the east.

In Moab, Naomi's husband died. Her sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then both sons died too. Naomi heard that there was food again in Bethlehem. She decided to go home. Her sons' wives started out with her.

On the road, Naomi told them to go back. Orpah went back. Ruth stayed. When they reached Bethlehem, the women of the town were surprised. Naomi told them not to call her Naomi, which means pleasant. She said to call her Mara, which means bitter. Her life had been very hard.

words.d: a Moabite woman who stayed with Naomi; also the short book that tells her story
Ruth's mother-in-law, who went to Moab in a famine and came home to Bethlehem
a land east of the Dead Sea; the book of Ruth says Naomi's family lived there

look.title: Pleasant or Bitter?
look.text: In Hebrew, the name Naomi is close to a word meaning pleasant. When Naomi comes home, she says: Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, which means bitter. Picture the women of Bethlehem hearing this. They knew her years ago, when she left with a husband and two sons. Now she is back with one young woman from Moab.
look.prompt: Why does Naomi want a new name? What has changed for her? What has she not lost?

check.q: Why did Naomi's family leave Bethlehem, according to the book of Ruth?
choices: They wanted to see the sea
check.why: Ruth 1:1 says there was a famine in the land, and the family went to Moab to find food.

check.q: Where was Moab?
check.why: Moab was a land east of the Dead Sea, across from Judah.

check.q: What name does Naomi ask to be called when she comes home?
check.why: Naomi says to call her Mara, which means bitter, because her life had been so hard.

lessons.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
lessons.mainIdea: Ruth's promise to Naomi is one of the best-known lines in the Tanakh, and Jewish tradition reads it as a choice to join the people of Israel.
reading: On the road, Ruth made a *promise*. She said she would go where Naomi went. She would live where Naomi lived. Naomi's people would be her people. Naomi's God would be her God. She would die where Naomi died. Only death would part them.

Ruth was a Moabite. She was not born into the people of Israel. Jewish tradition reads her words as a choice to join them. The rabbis of the Talmud and the midrash saw Ruth as a model of a person who becomes Jewish by choice. In Hebrew, such a person is called a *ger*.

Many readers notice what Ruth puts first. She does not say she will get a better life. She says she will stay with Naomi. Loyalty comes before anything else. The book of Ruth never uses the word love for the two women. It shows it instead.

words.d: words that bind you to do something; Ruth's promise was to stay with Naomi
in Jewish tradition, a person who joins the Jewish people by choice; Ruth is a model

look.title: Ruth's Promise
look.text: And Ruth said: 'Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God;
look.prompt: "Entreat" means beg. "Whither" means where. Count how many things Ruth promises in this one verse.

check.q: What does Ruth promise Naomi in Ruth 1:16?
choices: To go where she goes and stay with her
check.why: Ruth 1:16 says where you go, I will go, and your people shall be my people.

check.q: In Jewish tradition, what is a ger?
choices: A person who joins the Jewish people by choice
check.why: A ger is a person who becomes Jewish by choice. The rabbis read Ruth as a model of one.

check.q: What comes first in Ruth's promise, as many readers notice?
check.why: Ruth does not ask for anything for herself. She says she will stay with Naomi no matter what.

lessons.title: Gleaning in the Fields
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ruth says Ruth gathered leftover grain, a practice the Torah set up to feed the poor, in the field of a man named Boaz.
reading: Ruth and Naomi came to Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. They had no food. Ruth said she would go *glean*. To glean is to pick up grain that the harvesters drop or leave behind. The Torah says farmers must leave some grain for the poor and the stranger.

Ruth went to a field. It belonged to a man named *Boaz*. He was a relative of Naomi's husband. Boaz noticed Ruth. He had heard how she stayed with Naomi. He told his workers to let her glean safely. He told them to drop extra grain on purpose.

Ruth worked all day. She came home with a big load of barley. Naomi asked whose field it was. When she heard the name Boaz, she was glad. Boaz was family. In the book, gleaning is not just about food. It shows how the Torah's laws about the poor worked in a real field.

words.d: to gather grain left behind by harvesters; the Torah says it is for the poor and the stranger
the field owner in the book of Ruth, a relative of Naomi's husband
a grain harvested in spring; Ruth gleaned barley in Boaz's field

look.title: Leave Some for the Poor
look.text: Leviticus 19:9–10 tells farmers not to harvest all the way to the corners of their fields, and not to go back for what was dropped. The corners and the fallen grain are to be left for the poor and for the stranger.
look.cite: Leviticus (Vayikra) 19:9–10, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: Ruth was both poor and a stranger. How does this law from the Torah help explain what she does in Boaz's field?

check.q: What does it mean to glean?
choices: To sell grain at a market
To gather grain the harvesters left behind
check.why: Gleaning is picking up leftover grain. The Torah says it must be left for the poor and the stranger.

check.q: Who owned the field where Ruth gleaned?
check.why: Ruth 2 says the field belonged to Boaz, a relative of Naomi's husband.

check.q: What did Boaz tell his workers to do for Ruth?
check.why: Boaz told his workers to let Ruth glean safely and to leave extra grain for her.

lessons.title: Boaz the Redeemer
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Ruth says Boaz acted as a redeemer, married Ruth, and their great-grandson was King David.
reading: In the Torah, a close relative could help a family that lost its land or its men. Such a helper was called a *go'el*, a redeemer. Naomi knew Boaz was a relative. She sent Ruth to ask him to be their redeemer. Ruth went at night to the threshing floor, where grain was beaten out.

Boaz said he was willing. But there was a closer relative. Boaz went to the town gate, where business was done. He asked the other man in front of ten elders. The man said no. So Boaz took off his sandal, an old sign of a deal, and agreed to redeem the family.

Boaz married Ruth. They had a son named *Obed*. The women of the town said a son had been born to Naomi. The book ends with a family list. Obed was the father of Jesse. Jesse was the father of David. So Ruth, the stranger from Moab, was the great-grandmother of Israel's most famous king.

words.d: a redeemer; a close relative who helps a family that has lost its land or its men
the son of Ruth and Boaz; the book says he was the grandfather of David

look.title: From Ruth to David
look.text: Read the chain at the end of the book of Ruth like a set of steps. Ruth and Boaz have a son, Obed. Obed has a son, Jesse. Jesse has a son, David. David becomes the king remembered in the Psalms. Now go back to the dusty road. Ruth, a Moabite, was told to go home.
look.prompt: Why might the book end with this family list? What does it say about who can belong to the people of Israel?

check.q: What is a go'el?
choices: A redeemer, a relative who helps a family
check.why: A go'el is a redeemer. Boaz took on that role for Naomi and Ruth.

check.q: Where did Boaz settle the matter with the closer relative?
choices: At the town gate, in front of elders
check.why: Ruth 4 says Boaz went to the town gate, where business was done, and spoke before ten elders.

check.q: How is Ruth related to King David, according to the book?
check.why: The book ends: Obed, son of Ruth, was the father of Jesse, who was the father of David.

lessons.title: Ruth and Shavuot
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition reads the book of Ruth on Shavuot, the spring harvest holiday that also remembers the giving of the Torah.
reading: In the Tanakh, the book of Ruth is not next to Judges. It is in *Ketuvim*, the Writings, the third part. It is one of five short books called the *Megillot*, or scrolls. Each of the five is read on a different holiday. Ruth is read on *Shavuot*.

Shavuot comes seven weeks after Passover. Its name means weeks. It was a harvest holiday for wheat and the first fruits. Jewish tradition also says the Torah was given at Mount Sinai on Shavuot. Many Jewish families eat dairy foods, like cheese blintzes, on this day.

Why read Ruth on Shavuot? Readers give a few reasons. The story happens during the harvest. Ruth chose to accept the Torah, just as the people did at Sinai. And Jewish tradition says King David, Ruth's great-grandson, was born and died on Shavuot. In Chicago and around the world, synagogues read this scroll each spring.

words.d: the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh; the book of Ruth is in it
five short books in Ketuvim, each read on a holiday; Ruth is one of them
the holiday seven weeks after Passover; the harvest and the giving of the Torah

look.title: Counting to Shavuot
look.cite: Leviticus 23:15–16, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917; common Jewish practice
look.prompt: Seven weeks is forty-nine days. What number day is Shavuot? Why might a harvest holiday be a good day to read a story about a field?

check.q: In which part of the Tanakh is the book of Ruth?
check.why: Ruth is in Ketuvim, the third part, as one of the five Megillot, not next to Judges.

check.q: On which holiday is the book of Ruth read?
check.why: Jewish tradition reads Ruth on Shavuot, the harvest holiday seven weeks after Passover.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition say happened on Shavuot at Mount Sinai?
check.why: Jewish tradition teaches that the Torah was given at Sinai on Shavuot.

lessons.title: Hannah's Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: The first book of Samuel says Hannah prayed quietly for a child, and the rabbis made her prayer a model for how to pray.
reading: The book of *1 Samuel* begins with a woman named *Hannah*. She was married to Elkanah. She had no children. This made her very sad. Every year the family went to the holy place at Shiloh. One year, Hannah went to the door of the sanctuary and prayed.

Hannah made a promise. If God gave her a son, she would give him back to serve God all his life. She prayed with her lips moving, but no sound came out. The priest *Eli* saw her. He thought she was drunk. Hannah said no. She was pouring out her heart.

Eli blessed her. The text says Hannah had a son. She named him *Samuel*. When he was a small boy, she brought him to Shiloh to live with Eli, as she had promised. The rabbis of the Talmud pointed to Hannah. They said prayer should be like hers: quiet, from the heart, with the lips moving.

words.d: the woman in 1 Samuel who prayed for a son and promised him to God
the priest at Shiloh who blessed Hannah and raised Samuel
Hannah's son, who became a prophet and judge; also the name of two books in Nevi'im

look.title: How Hannah Prayed
look.text: In the Talmud, tractate Berakhot 31a, the rabbis learn rules for prayer from Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:13. She spoke in her heart, so a person praying should mean it inside. Her lips moved, so a person should form the words. Her voice was not heard, so prayer should be quiet.
look.cite: Talmud, Berakhot 31a, paraphrased from Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903; 1 Samuel 1:13, JPS 1917
look.prompt: The rabbis turned a story into rules. Find each rule and the part of Hannah's story it comes from.

check.q: What did Hannah promise if she had a son?
choices: To bring him a new coat
To give him back to serve God
check.why: 1 Samuel 1:11 says Hannah promised to give her son to serve God all his life.

check.q: What did Eli think when he saw Hannah praying?
check.why: Eli saw her lips move with no sound and thought she was drunk; she told him she was pouring out her heart.

check.q: Why do the rabbis of the Talmud point to Hannah?
choices: Her prayer is a model: quiet and from the heart
check.why: Berakhot 31a learns rules for prayer from how Hannah prayed in 1 Samuel 1.

lessons.title: A Voice in the Night
lessons.mainIdea: The text says young Samuel heard a voice calling his name at night, and Eli taught him how to answer.
reading: Samuel grew up at Shiloh. He helped Eli, who was old and could not see well. One night Samuel was lying down near the *ark*, the holy box that held the tablets. He heard a voice call his name. He ran to Eli and said, here I am. Eli said he had not called.

This happened three times. The third time, Eli understood. He told Samuel to lie down again. If the voice came, Samuel should say: speak, for your servant is listening. The voice came a fourth time. Samuel answered as Eli had said.

The text says the message was hard. Eli's sons had done wrong, and Eli had not stopped them. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli. In the morning, Eli made him tell everything. Eli accepted it. From then on, the book says, all Israel knew Samuel was a *prophet*, a person who speaks for God.

words.d: here, the holy box at Shiloh that held the tablets; not Noah's boat
a person the text says speaks for God; Samuel became one

look.title: Speak, I Am Listening
look.text: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times: 'Samuel, Samuel.' Then Samuel said: 'Speak; for Thy servant heareth.'
look.prompt: "Heareth" means hears. Who taught Samuel to answer this way? Why might it matter that he says he is listening, not talking?

check.q: Where was Samuel when he heard the voice, according to 1 Samuel 3?
check.why: 1 Samuel 3 says Samuel was lying down in the sanctuary at Shiloh, where the ark was.

check.q: Who told Samuel how to answer the voice?
check.why: The third time, Eli understood and told Samuel to say: speak, for your servant is listening.

check.q: What is a prophet in the Tanakh?
choices: A person who speaks for God
check.why: A prophet is someone the text says speaks for God. After that night, all Israel knew Samuel as a prophet.

lessons.title: Samuel the Judge
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Samuel was the last of the judges, traveling from town to town to lead the people.
reading: Samuel grew up to be a judge, like Deborah and Gideon. But he was also a prophet. The book says he traveled in a circle each year. He went to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah. In each place he judged the people. Then he went home to Ramah.

The Philistines were still a danger. The text says they once captured the ark in battle. Eli died when he heard the news. Later, Samuel gathered the people at *Mizpah*. He prayed for them. The text says the Philistines were driven back.

Samuel set up a stone to remember that day. He called it Eben-ezer, which means stone of help. Readers often call Samuel the last judge. After him, the book turns to kings. Jewish tradition counts 1 and 2 Samuel as two parts of one book, named for him.

words.d: the town where the text says Samuel gathered the people and prayed
stone of help; the name Samuel gave a stone to remember a victory

look.title: Samuel's Yearly Circle
look.prompt: Why might a judge travel to different towns instead of staying in one place? Think about who could reach him.

check.q: What did Samuel do in Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah each year?
check.why: 1 Samuel 7:16 says Samuel went in a circle to these towns and judged Israel in each place.

check.q: What does Eben-ezer mean?
check.why: Samuel named the stone Eben-ezer, stone of help, to remember the victory at Mizpah.

check.q: Why do readers call Samuel the last judge?
choices: After him, the book turns to kings
check.why: Samuel led as a judge, and then, 1 Samuel says, the people asked for a king.

sections.title: The People Ask for a King

lessons.title: Give Us a King
lessons.mainIdea: The book of 1 Samuel says the people asked Samuel for a king like other nations, and Samuel warned them what a king would take.
reading: Samuel grew old. His sons were judges, but the text says they were not honest. The elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah. They said: give us a king to judge us, like all the *nations*. Samuel did not like this. He prayed about it.

The text says God told Samuel to listen to the people. But Samuel should warn them first. So Samuel told them what a king would do. A king would take their sons for his army. He would take their daughters as workers. He would take the best of their fields and a tenth of their crops.

The people still said they wanted a king. They wanted someone to lead them in battle. Samuel agreed. Later, the text says, he poured oil on the head of a tall young man named *Saul*. This was called anointing. Saul became the first king. The next chapter tells his story.

words.d: other peoples with their own lands and rulers; Israel asked for a king like theirs
the tall young man the text says Samuel anointed as Israel's first king
to pour oil on someone's head as a sign they are chosen to lead

look.title: What a King Will Take
look.text: In 1 Samuel 8:11–17, Samuel warns the people. A king will take their sons to drive his chariots and run before him. He will take their daughters to cook and bake. He will take the best fields and vineyards and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of their grain and flocks. And the people, Samuel says, will be his servants.
look.cite: 1 Samuel 8:11–17, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: The people heard this warning and still wanted a king. Why do you think they did? Was Samuel right to warn them?

check.q: What did the elders ask Samuel for?
check.why: 1 Samuel 8:5 says the elders asked for a king to judge them, like all the nations.

check.q: What did Samuel warn a king would do?
choices: Take their sons, daughters, fields and crops
check.why: In 1 Samuel 8, Samuel lists what a king takes: sons, daughters, fields and a tenth of the crops.

check.q: What does it mean to anoint someone?
choices: To pour oil on their head as a sign they are chosen
check.why: Anointing means pouring oil on the head. The text says Samuel anointed Saul as the first king.

lessons.title: Chesed, the Thread
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word chesed, loyal kindness, runs through the stories of Ruth, Hannah and Samuel.
reading: There is a Hebrew word that runs through this chapter. The word is *chesed*. It is hard to say in one English word. It means kindness, but more than that. It means kindness that keeps a promise. It means loyalty. The JPS 1917 translation often says kindness or mercy.

The book of Ruth uses the word three times. Naomi hopes God will show chesed to Ruth and Orpah. Naomi says Boaz has shown chesed to the living and the dead. Boaz tells Ruth her chesed is great. Ruth stayed when she did not have to. That is chesed.

Hannah kept her promise and gave up her son. Eli accepted hard news with grace. Samuel served the people all his life. Jewish tradition calls chesed one of the things the world stands on, in Pirkei Avot 1:2. Readers say the book of Ruth is a story of chesed from start to end.

words.d: loyal kindness; kindness that keeps a promise even when it costs something
staying true to a person or a promise, the way Ruth stayed with Naomi

look.title: What the World Stands On
look.text: In Pirkei Avot 1:2, Simeon the Just is quoted as saying the world stands on three things: on the Torah, on worship, and on acts of loving-kindness, in Hebrew gemilut chasadim.
look.cite: Pirkei Avot 1:2, paraphrased from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Pick one person from this chapter. Which of the three things in this saying did they do? Give one example from the text.

check.q: What does chesed mean?
choices: Loyal kindness that keeps a promise
check.why: Chesed is kindness joined with loyalty, like Ruth staying with Naomi when she did not have to.

check.q: Who does Boaz say has shown great chesed?
check.why: In Ruth 3, Boaz tells Ruth that her kindness, her chesed, is great.

check.q: In Pirkei Avot 1:2, what are the three things the world stands on?
choices: Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness
check.why: Simeon the Just's saying names Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim.

review.q: Why did Naomi's family go to Moab?
review.why: Ruth 1:1 says a famine sent the family from Bethlehem to Moab.

review.q: Which of these is part of Ruth's promise in Ruth 1:16?
choices: I will build you a house
Your people shall be my people
I will go back to Moab
review.why: Ruth says: where you go, I will go; your people shall be my people; your God, my God.

review.q: Who was the great-grandson of Ruth and Boaz?
review.why: The book of Ruth ends: Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.

review.q: On which holiday do Jewish communities read the book of Ruth?
review.why: Ruth, one of the five Megillot, is read on Shavuot, the harvest holiday.

review.q: How did Hannah pray at Shiloh?
review.why: 1 Samuel 1:13 says Hannah spoke in her heart; her lips moved but her voice was not heard.

review.q: What did Eli tell Samuel to say to the voice?
choices: Speak, for your servant is listening
Where you go, I will go
review.why: 1 Samuel 3:9 says Eli told Samuel to answer: speak, for Thy servant heareth.

review.q: Whom did Samuel anoint as the first king of Israel?
review.why: 1 Samuel 10 says Samuel anointed Saul, a tall young man, as Israel's first king.

review.q: Which word best describes Ruth staying with Naomi?
review.why: Boaz calls Ruth's loyalty chesed, kindness that keeps a promise at a cost.
